issues.legal_issue: A final writ direction granting additional equitable compensation cannot be reopened in later land-acquisition reference or appellate proceedings between the same parties or their privies when it has been acted upon and was not challenged.
material_facts: A final writ order directed payment of equitable interest from the date possession was taken, in addition to statutory compensation and interest.
The direction applied to the affected landowners, was acted upon, and was reflected in the Land Acquisition Officer’s award.
The State did not challenge the writ direction or the award granting the additional interest.
The later reference and appeal concerned compensation for the acquired land, and the High Court displaced the additional interest despite the prior final direction.
issues.conclusion: The prior direction and the award granting the additional interest had attained finality and could not be reopened; the Reference Court and the High Court in its appellate jurisdiction could not revisit that question.
issues.legal_principle: The rule of res judicata, including cause-of-action and issue estoppel, applies between proceedings and at later stages of the same proceedings, including writ proceedings under Article 226. Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure embodies the rule’s purpose of conclusively settling issues and preventing renewed litigation. The Court relied on Hope Plantations Ltd. v. Taluk Land Board, Swamy Atmananda v. Sri Ramakrishna Tapovanam, Gulabchand Chhotalal Parikh v. State of Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh Road Transport Corporation v. Balwant Singh, Bhanu Kumar Jain v. Archana Kumar, Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Deorajin Debi, Prahlad Singh v. Sukhdev Singh, Y.B. Patil, and Ishwardas v. State of Madhya Pradesh. Sections 18 and 54 of the Land Acquisition Act concern reference and appellate proceedings, but did not authorize reopening the final direction in these proceedings.

rule.if: land_acquisition_reference_or_appeal and prior_final_writ_order and same_compensation_issue and prior_order_implemented and no_challenge_to_prior_order

predicates.land_acquisition_reference_or_appeal: The proceeding is a reference or appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.prior_final_writ_order: A court previously made a final writ order concerning the compensation now in dispute.
predicates.same_compensation_issue: The later proceeding concerns the same compensation issue determined by the earlier order.
predicates.prior_order_implemented: The party bound by the earlier order acted in accordance with it.
predicates.no_challenge_to_prior_order: The party bound by the earlier order did not challenge it through an available procedure.

issues.definition: When a land-acquisition reference or appeal concerns the same compensation issue determined by a final writ order that was implemented and not challenged, the earlier equitable-compensation direction remains binding and cannot be reopened.

issues.legal_issue: A final writ of mandamus must be obeyed unless it is overruled or legislation changes the legal position in a way that displaces it.
material_facts: The High Court issued a writ of mandamus directing payment of equitable interest to affected landowners.
The direction became final and was acted upon.
No judgment overruling the direction or legislation displacing it was identified.
The later appellate judgment was inconsistent with the direction and the resulting award.
issues.conclusion: The final writ of mandamus remained binding and had to be obeyed; the later proceedings could not be used to disregard it.
issues.legal_principle: A final mandamus is binding unless overruled or displaced by legislation; an order giving effect to a right by mandamus cannot simply be disregarded while it stands. The Court relied on Madan Mohan Pathak v. Union of India, which explains that any remedy against such a judgment lies through procedures such as appeal or review, not disobedience.

rule.if: proceeding_seeks_to_disregard_mandamus and mandamus_is_final and not mandamus_overruled and not_displacing_legislation_enacted

predicates.proceeding_seeks_to_disregard_mandamus: A later proceeding would disregard or contradict a court’s direction issued by mandamus.
predicates.mandamus_overruled: A later court judgment has overruled the mandamus.
predicates.not_displacing_legislation_enacted: No legislation has changed the legal position so as to displace the mandamus.

issues.definition: When a later proceeding would disregard a final mandamus and neither a judgment has overruled it nor legislation has displaced it, the mandamus must be obeyed.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court cannot decide a case on a ground outside the parties’ pleadings or make out a new case that was not raised by them.
material_facts: The State’s appeal did not raise the question whether the equitable interest directed by the earlier writ order could be granted.
The High Court relied on a decision concerning the availability of equitable interest and used that issue to set aside the additional interest.
The issue on which the High Court ruled had not been raised by the State.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not go outside the pleadings and make out a new case; its decision on the unraised issue was erroneous.
issues.legal_principle: Although Section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives an appellate court broad powers, a decision must remain within the case pleaded by the parties. The Court relied on Siddu Venkappa Devadiga v. Rangu S. Devadiga, which cites Trojan and Co. Ltd. v. R.M.N.N. Nagappa Chettiar and Raruha Singh v. Achal Singh for the rule that a decision cannot rest on grounds outside the parties’ pleas.

predicates.statutory_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a decision made in a statutory proceeding.
predicates.issue_not_raised_in_pleadings: The parties did not raise the issue in their pleadings or submissions.
predicates.appellate_court_decides_unpleaded_issue: The appellate court decides the appeal on that unraised issue.

issues.definition: When an appellate court decides a statutory appeal on an issue the parties did not raise, it must not decide the appeal on that unpleaded issue.
